tagline.text: The last home of revolutionary Apolinario Mabini, preserved on the PUP campus in Manila

location.label: Location
location.text: Inside the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) Mabini Campus, Santa Mesa, Manila

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Dry season November–April (the museum is open Tuesday to Sunday year-round)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–600 (transport and snacks, check the admission fee locally, starting from central Manila)

children.text: A national shrine on the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) campus in Santa Mesa, Manila, it preserves the bamboo-and-nipa house where Apolinario Mabini, known as the Brains of the Revolution, died in 1903. It closed for restoration in September 2023 and reopened on December 10, 2025.

The Mabini Shrine stands inside the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) Mabini Campus in the Santa Mesa district of Manila. Its Filipino name is Dambanang Apolinario Mabini, and the museum side is called Museo ni Apolinario Mabini-PUP. It is a national shrine managed by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), and its core is the bamboo house with a nipa palm roof where Mabini spent the later part of his life and died of cholera on May 13, 1903. The house did not always stand here; it was moved several times as the city grew before settling on this site. Because it sits inside a university, you may need to ask for directions to the shrine at the entrance, and entry hours may differ on days when the school holds events.
Apolinario Mabini was a lawyer and revolutionary born in Tanauan, Batangas, on

. He contracted polio in 1895 and by around January 1896 had lost the use of both legs, yet he served as adviser and, in effect, first prime minister of Aguinaldo's revolutionary government, and wrote the 1898 constitutional program (Programa Constitucional de la República Filipina) and "The True Decalogue." That is why he is still called the Brains of the Revolution. He was captured by US forces in December 1899, refused to pledge allegiance to the United States, was exiled to Guam, and returned in February 1903. He died in this house three months after coming home. As a place that honors a statesman's final days, the mood is less about spectacle and more about quietly reflecting on the man.

Knowing how the house traveled makes the site more interesting. According to English Wikipedia, the house originally stood at 21 Calle Nagtahan on the north bank of the Pasig River, and Mabini lived there from 1888. In the 1930s it was moved next door to No. 23 to make way for the Nagtahan Bridge (now the Mabini Bridge), and in 1960 it was moved again, to the Bureau of Animal Industry compound in Malacañang Park, so that the bridge could be widened. Architect Juan Nakpil supervised the restoration then. In 1968 Proclamation No. 324 made it a national shrine, and in 2007 a Pasig River widening plan again threatened another move, with the PUP campus and Arroceros Park among the proposed sites. In 2010, Proclamation No. 1992 made the PUP Mabini Campus its permanent home, and restoration continued until around 2013. From September 2023, the shrine was closed to visitors for building conservation and improvements to exhibition and office space. After a roughly two-year restoration and museum enhancement project it reopened on December 10, 2025, and the reopening was reported as the first step of a 10-year NHCP program to renovate the 28 shrines, landmarks, and museums under its care. PUP's official news says it is now open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., while some older NHCP listings give 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., so please check the latest announcement before you go.

For travelers, this is a historic site you can fit into half a day in Manila. It is not crowded with tourists the way Intramuros is, so you can see it quietly. Because it is on a university campus, there are many students on weekdays during the school term, and the gate may check ID. If you know a little about modern Philippine history, you will appreciate why Mabini matters far more. Think of it as a calm visit to one small house and its exhibits rather than a large museum. On your first visit, ask at the PUP gate for directions to the shrine, then check with shrine staff which areas are open and what the photo rules are, and you will not get lost. Groups and student field trips may need reservations, so it is safer to contact the NHCP in advance. Unlike older reviews, the exhibits and routes may have changed after the reopening, so treat the exhibit descriptions here as a guide and follow the signs on site.

blocks.title: The bamboo-and-nipa house where Mabini died

children.text: The heart of the shrine is the house where Mabini died on May 13, 1903. It is a traditional bahay kubo built of bamboo and nipa palm leaves, said to have been dismantled and rebuilt to its original design. A 2014 visitor account describes two bedrooms, a kitchen, a living room (sala), and an antesala (reception room). Because the house is a heritage structure, rules about footwear and access may apply, so follow the staff's instructions.

blocks.title: The study-reception room and the convalescent chair

children.text: Mabini died in the antesala, which also served as his study. A 2014 visitor account says his convalescent chair is on display. The best part of the visit is imagining a man who could not use his legs sitting here and carrying on prime-ministerial work. The reopening may have changed the exhibit layout, so check the explanations on site.

blocks.title: The renovated Museo ni Apolinario Mabini

children.text: The museum, a short distance from the house, is known to display items Mabini used, his writings, and quotations on the walls. Reports say new exhibits were installed in the 2025 improvement project, but I could not confirm the specific exhibit list. An older visitor account also mentions a small section on the Philippine-American War.

blocks.title: The hammock display and Mabini's illness

children.text: A 2014 visitor account mentions a reproduction hammock that represents Mabini's use of one after he lost the use of his legs. It recalls how he kept working in government and writing despite his physical condition. It is the most direct display of a person who overcame the limits of his body.

blocks.title: The history of a house that moved many times

children.text: The story of the house, from Calle Nagtahan through Malacañang Park to PUP, is a miniature of Manila's urban development. If you ask the signage or the staff, you can learn how the house was pushed from place to place by bridge and river widening. PUP is now designated as its permanent home.

blocks.title: The PUP campus and its Pasig riverside atmosphere

children.text: The Mabini Campus lies on the Pasig riverbank and is lively with students. After seeing the shrine, a campus walk gives you a light taste of Manila's university district. The school sets its own entry rules, so bag checks and ID requests are possible.

blocks.title: The Mabini Bridge and the Santa Mesa neighborhood

children.text: The Mabini Bridge (formerly the Nagtahan Bridge) is named after the address of Mabini's old house. If you see the shrine first and then the bridge and riverside streets, you will understand why the house had to be moved so many times. The roads are busy, so check a map app for a safe walking route.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The shrine, the museum, and a stroll through the university district

children.text: Get off at LRT-2 Pureza station or PNR Santa Mesa station and go to the gate of the PUP Mabini Campus. Tell the security staff you are visiting the shrine and follow their directions.
Arrive at opening time and look slowly at the exterior of the Mabini Shrine. Take note of the nipa roof and the bamboo structure.
Go inside and see the bedroom, kitchen, and reception room in turn. Spend a quiet moment in the reception room where Mabini died.
Walk to the museum and read the exhibits and the quotations on the walls. Check whether there is a section on the Philippine-American War.
Have a simple lunch at a campus eatery or on a Santa Mesa street.
Take a taxi or LRT-2 to other Manila sights such as Malacañang Palace or Quiapo Church.
The opening time is announced as
, so it is best not to arrive too early. The shrine is known to be closed on Mondays, so visit between Tuesday and Sunday.
Get off at LRT-2 Pureza station and head toward PUP. The PNR Santa Mesa station is close to Pureza station, so you can also use PNR and get off at the nearer station.
From Pureza station you can walk to the campus or take a tricycle or jeepney. Check a map app for the exact gate and the travel time.
An old PUP guide describes a route of changing to a tricycle and a jeepney from Pureza station, getting off at Teresa Street, and walking, but that information is outdated.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport, a taxi or Grab to PUP takes about
40–90 minutes
. The time varies greatly with traffic.
You can also transfer between LRT-1 and LRT-2, but with luggage a taxi is recommended.
From central Manila (Ermita and Malate), a taxi or Grab is convenient.
A PUP ferry station on the Pasig River Ferry Service is said to be near the campus, but check locally whether it is operating.
The shrine is mainly an indoor visit, so the season matters little. The dry season simply makes walking around the campus more comfortable.
In the rainy season, roads around Santa Mesa can flood, so avoid the hours of heavy showers.

Rather than staying near the shrine, it is more convenient to base yourself in downtown Manila in Malate, Ermita, or Makati. Santa Mesa is a student district and has few large hotels.
For meals, use the local eateries and food courts around the campus and the fast-food outlets along Santa Mesa streets. If hygiene worries you, choose a large chain.
Check the opening hours again on the NHCP or PUP official announcements before you go. Operations may change so soon after the reopening.
Bring your passport or an ID, which helps when entering the campus.
The shrine is known to be closed on Mondays, so go between Tuesday and Sunday.
The house is a heritage structure, so do not touch or lean on it, and ask staff whether photography is allowed.
Reading about Mabini's life beforehand makes the visit far more meaningful. This is a different place from the Mabini Shrine in Tanauan.
You will sweat a lot in the hot daytime, so bring water and a small towel.
The shrine reopened only recently, so the opening hours and fees may change; check the official announcements before you visit.
Traffic around Santa Mesa is heavy and pickpockets may be about, so watch your phone and wallet.
Because it is a university campus, entry may be restricted during school events or exam periods.
Roads can flood in the rainy season, so check the weather.
Ask a map app and the security staff which entrance is closest to the shrine.
A historic site close to the Malacañang Park area where Mabini's old house once stood. Try taking a taxi there.
A historic campus in the Sampaloc side of the same Manila university district, where you can compare the campus atmosphere.
The main church of old Manila, easy to reach by continuing on LRT-2.
The center of Manila's historical travel, which you can continue to in a half-day itinerary after visiting the shrine.
